title: ATL
full_review:
Unless you hail from a certain ZIP code, you may not know that the cryptic title of director Chris Robinson's film "ATL" (Warner Bros.) refers to the slang abbreviation for Atlanta.

Loosely inspired by the experiences of the movie's producers, Dallas Austin and Tionne "T-Boz" Watkins, and based on a story by Antwone Fisher (whose own life was adapted to the screen in a movie bearing his name), the familiar but satisfying coming-of-age-in-the-'hood drama centers on Rashad (rapper Tip Harris), a 17-year-old aspiring graphic artist forced to raise himself and wayward kid brother Ant (Evan Ross) after their parents' death.

Their embittered Uncle George (Mykelti Williamson), who "lets" them live under his roof and earn some money helping out with his janitorial service, is not much help, leaving Rashad to shoulder most of the load, a burden further complicated by Ant's falling in with a local drug dealer and his own budding, star-crossed romance with a girl (Lauren London) whose sass masks a secret.

His only escape is roller skating at a popular rink with his crew, including best friend Esquire (Jackie Long) who has his sights set on the Ivy League.

Despite a cliched script, "ATL" is visually vibrant and wins over your emotions with its appealing performances and positive themes about the bonds of family and friendship, owning up to responsibilities, holding on to dreams and taking pride in your roots.

The film contains some violence and sexual situations, including an implied encounter between minors, suggestive roller-skating choreography, drug content, an instance of rough language and some crude language and humor. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
